catalog_quote: My spelling of Malagasy words and sounds largely follows the official spelling, except for ‘o’ which is written as u, final ‘y’ which is written as i, and the indication of stress on words of more than one syllable. Moreover, final vowels sometimes obtain a brève sign and are written as ă, ĭ, or ŭ. My reasons for this are that both ‘i’ and ‘y’ stand for the same phoneme, the pronunciation of orthographic ‘o’ is closer to [u] than to [o], some final vowels are whispered, and Malagasy stress is contrastive. [p.60] ... Table 4. Polite body-part terms in Tandroy ... Anus fùri fiambesàraŋĕ ... Belly trùkĕ fisafùaŋĕ ... Ear sùfi(ñĕ) ravembìa ... Eye màsu fihaìnu ... Foot, leg tùmbukĕ fandìa ... Hand tàŋa(ñĕ) fìta ... Head lùha ambùne, aŋambùne ... Head hair vùlu marùi ... Heart fu arùfu ... Lip sùŋi fivìmbi ... Mouth vàva falìe ... Name aŋàraŋĕ tahìnaŋĕ ... Nose urù(ñĕ) fi-antsùnaŋĕ ... Penis làtakĕ, vùtu filahìaŋĕ ... Private parts - fiheŋàraŋĕ ... Saliva ìve rànu-palìe ... Tongue lèla famèle ... Tooth nìfe fihìtsi ... Urine amàni arirànu ... Vagina ìsi fivavèŋĕ [pp.80-81]

[...] [The thesis] first describes the phonetics and phonology of the Tandroy dialect and shows that the Tandroy dialect has stress rules and that these are involved in the formation of imperative sentences. Clarifying the interface between these stress rules and syntactic structure is one of the major achievements of this thesis.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (text read in full). Abstract p.1 (続紙1) has '第 3 章は Tandroy 方言 の 音声と強勢規則について述べる。' and examiners' report p.3 (続紙2) has 'まず Tandroy 方言の音声と音韻に つ いて述べ、Tandroy 方言には強勢規則があり、これ が命令文形成に係っていることを明 らかに し た。この 強 勢規 則と 統 語構 造と の イン ター フ ェー スの 解 明は 、本 論 文の 大き な功績 の 1つ であ る。' -- identical to the reported quote apart from PDF-extraction whitespace and the [..] joining two pages; translation is accurate. It indeed says only that Tandroy HAS stress rules (interacting with imperative formation), not where stress falls. On the identity of the variety: all Nishimoto items are Tandroy of Androy (far south, ~500k speakers), i.e. tand1256 (Glottolog 'Tandroy-Mahafaly Malagasy', ISO…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only openly readable first-hand text asserts that Tandroy has rule-governed word stress that shifts under (imperative) suffixation, but does not say where stress falls. The actual rule is in Nishimoto 2018 §1.3.3 (pp.33-38), Nishimoto 2010 (Interlingüística 21) and thesis ch.3, none accessible; the section layout (weak endings -ke/-tse/-ñe treated together with the stress rule) and Howe 2017's pan-Malagasy summary (penultimate stress, antepenultimate with weak final syllables -ke/-tse in southwestern dialects, citing Dahl 1952) suggest the standard Malagasy pattern, but no opened source states this for Tandroy.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift in imperative formation (abstract); weak endings -ke, -tse, -ñe have their own section adjacent to the stress rule in Nishimoto 2018 (ToC only).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress rules interacting with verbal morphology (imperatives); no phrase-level information accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: All Nishimoto sources describe Tandroy as spoken in Androy (fieldwork around Ambovombe/Amboasary region, far south); Glottolog tand1256 'Tandroy-Mahafaly Malagasy' also subsumes Mahafaly and Karimbola, which these works do not cover. Rajaonarimanana & Fee 1996 is likewise Tandroy proper (spelled tañdroy).

All three quoted passages are there verbatim at the stated locators: spelling note 'My spelling of Malagasy words and sounds largely follows the official spelling, except for ‘o’ which is written as u, final ‘y’ which is written as i, and the indication of stress on words of more than one syllable. Moreover, final vowels sometimes obtain a brève sign.. some final vowels are whispered, and Malagasy stress is contrastive.' on the spread with footer '60 61' (p.5, i.e. p.60); '(1) the tendency to reduce ante-penultimate vowels (which as a rule precede the stressed syllable)' on the spread with f…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing 'fixed: penultimate' statement (taken from the Nishimoto 2011 abstract, whose quoted text actually only says a stress rule exists and figures in imperative formation, without giving the position). Adelaar's stress-marked Tandroy data are the first position evidence held by the project: penultimate on full-vowel-final words, antepenultimate on weak-final words, plus the pan-Malagasy remark that stress is contrastive. Not an explicit Tandroy rule statement; the reading is derived from marked data.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress rule is stated for Tandroy as such; the work only says (for Malagasy generally) that stress is contrastive and is marked on every polysyllable, and that antepenultimate vowels 'as a rule precede the stressed syllable'. Adelaar's own Tandroy fieldnote forms (consultant from Solapa, South Antanimora, p.86) carry a grave accent on the penultimate vowel of every word ending in a full vowel (màsu, lùha, nìfe, fandìa, marùi, ambùne, afèru, tsinài, sàndri, hàndri) and on the antepenult of words ending in a whispered/weak final -kĕ, -tsĕ, -ŋĕ, -ñĕ (trùkĕ, tùmbukĕ, làtakĕ, vàtaŋĕ, taùlaŋĕ, aŋàraŋĕ, tahìnaŋĕ, hùlitsĕ, ùzatsĕ, tùmitsĕ); an optional -ŋĕ/-ñĕ does not move the stress (sùfi(ñĕ), tàŋa(ŋĕ), ùru(ŋĕ)). So: penultimate stress counting the weak final syllable as extrametrical, i.e. the general Malagasy pattern.
new_statements.exceptions: Words with the weak final syllables -kĕ/-tsĕ/-ŋĕ/-ñĕ are marked with antepenultimate stress (the whispered final vowel does not count). Table 4 prints urù(ñĕ) 'nose' against ùru(ŋĕ) in the etymological list (p.64), apparently a slip. 'Malagasy stress is contrastive' is asserted for the language as a whole, not illustrated for Tandroy.
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar's Tandroy (TDR) data come from a single consultant, Andromasy Famantarantsoa, 25, from Solapa, South Antanimora, Tandroy region (July 2018; appendix p.86); Adelaar notes a few lexical differences between this variety and the Rajaonarimanana & Fee 1996 dictionary (e.g. 'sweat' fàna vs lìŋetsĕ), none concerning stress. He also cites Mahafaly (MFL) forms (tùmbukĕ, rànju) with the same stress placement.

new_statements.translation: [p.16] The main characteristic of this transcription is that it closely follows the spelling traditions of the official language while also trying to represent all the phonic particularities of Tandroy. [headwords] àba 'dad' | abèy expresses a complaint | àbi(ke) 'all' | aboàly 'termite mound' | abodỳ 'alphabet' | àda(ñe) (root) | àfake 'free, detached from' | afokàso(ke) 'match' | akànjo 'clothes (shirt or dress)' ... Imperative akanjò. akanjò raho! 'dress me!' | àkatse (root), akareñe 'that is taken out', Imperative akaro | alasỳ (< French scie) 'saw' | alìotse 'a swallow-like bird'.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Adelaar 2019, classification lexical: 'Malagasy stress is contrastive', stress-marked TDR forms) and the statements held by the project (read as fixed penultimate, antepenultimate on weak-final words; Nishimoto 2011 abstract: Tandroy has stress rules that interact with imperative formation): the dictionary's own headword accents show the same placements (penult default; antepenult before weak -ke/-tse/-ñe, which the dictionary parenthesises) and add two details: (a) a final-stressed class of loans and interjections (alasỳ, abodỳ, adabarà, alahasà, abèy), (b) stress shift to the final in the imperative (akànjo -> Imp. akanjò), consistent with Nishimoto's abstract. No contradi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The excerpt contains NO rule sentence on stress: §4 of the introduction breaks off at book p.17 (Remarques on final y/e and the glottal stop) and the accent paragraph, if the introduction has one, is on p.18 ff., outside the excerpt. What the excerpt does show, verbatim, is the dictionary's practice: every polysyllabic headword carries one grave accent on the stressed vowel (function words like ahy3 prép., 'ay2 unaccented). Over the c. 90 headwords of pp.33-38 the accent sits on the penult by default (àba, adàbo, adàla, adàlo, àfo, àhy, àja, ajàly, akàla, akànga, akòho, akòndro, alàma, alahàdy, akìba..), on the antepenult when the last syllable is a weak -ke/-tse/-ñe (àfake, àlike, àlake, akàhake, alènteke, àkatse, àhetse/àhitse, alìotse, ajàleñe; with the weak final parenthesised: àbi(ke), àda(ñe), àfe(ñe), ài(ñe), àle(ñe), alàla(ñe), afokàso(ke); but akatsìke/sakatsìke penult), and on the final syllable in a lexical class of Arabic/French loans and interjections (adabarà, alahasà, alimizandà, alasỳ < scie, abodỳ, abèy, alisày) and in imperatives (noun akànjo vs Imp. akanjò). Read as: penultimate default, antepenultimate with weak finals, a marked final class = the placement already held by the project; inferred from the marked forms, not from a statement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not marked: one grave accent per headword; derived forms and example phrases inside entries are mostly unaccented (except e.g. ajajalàhy, ajajampèla, akanjò, fiteñà, diribàna, akoholahin-tanà)
new_statements.exceptions: none stated (no rule text in the excerpt); observed in the data: final stress on loans/interjections and imperatives (akanjò), penult akatsìke despite final -ke
new_statements.identity_note: Tandroy (Antandroy) Malagasy of the Androy region, far south Madagascar; the dictionary describes the Tandroy dialect (Rajaonarimanana, INALCO; Fee, fieldwork in Androy).

sources.citation: Howe, Penelope. 2017. Tonogenesis in Central dialects of Malagasy. PhD dissertation, Rice University (hdl 1911/96031).
sources.note: §2.3.6 p.48: pan-Malagasy statement -- 'Most words have primary lexical stress on the penultimate syllable. However, lexical items ending in one of the weak final syllables (-na, -ka, -tra in Merina; -ke, -tse in western and southwestern dialects (Dahl 1952)..) have antepenultimate stress, and a small number of words have final-syllable stress.' Tandroy is placed in the Southwestern group (p.24) and Tandroy speakers (Amboasary) took part in her production study (word list Table C.9 pp.490-491, no stress marks), but there is no Tandroy-specific stress statement.
